name: The Madman Theory
statement: Seem unhinged enough to do the unthinkable, and adversaries may back down from threats a rational leader could never make credible.
statementAccent: threats a rational leader could never make credible
meaning: The madman theory is a coercive-bargaining strategy in which a leader deliberately cultivates a reputation for irrationality, volatility, or willingness to use extreme and disproportionate force, up to nuclear weapons, so that adversaries, fearing unpredictable and catastrophic escalation, back down or make concessions. Its logic is counterintuitive: a threat to escalate that would be suicidal for a rational leader is easy to dismiss, but the same threat becomes credible if the adversary believes the leader unhinged enough to carry it out. The madness is a performance staged for leverage, not a psychiatric condition.
mechanism: The strategy exploits a credibility inversion. In a world of mutual assured destruction, a rational leader's threat to escalate to catastrophe is not believable, since carrying it out would be self-defeating. By appearing irrational, obsessive, or unable to back down, a leader manufactures credibility for exactly such a threat. It rests on Cold War bargaining logic: Thomas Schelling showed that a bargainer can gain by worsening his own options and by the threat that leaves something to chance, manufacturing genuine risk of escalation to coerce an opponent, and the rationality of irrationality, associated with Herman Kahn, holds that a suicidal threat is credible only if irrationality is believed.

examples.text: By Haldeman's account, Nixon said he wanted the North Vietnamese to believe he might do anything to end the war, that he was obsessed and had his hand on the nuclear button, so they would beg for peace, though Nixon later denied the term.
Machiavelli praised Lucius Junius Brutus for feigning folly to survive and overthrow the Tarquins, calling it a very wise thing to simulate madness at the right time, an ancient antecedent.

Nixon and Kissinger's aborted Duck Hook escalation plan and a secret global nuclear alert are cited as attempts to operationalise the theory, and are widely judged to have failed to coerce Hanoi or Moscow.

variants.name: The threat that leaves something to chance
variants.text: Schelling's device of manufacturing genuine risk of accidental escalation, so that even an opponent who doubts a deliberate strike must weigh the chance of losing control.

variants.name: Feigned madness
variants.text: The older tradition, from Brutus through Machiavelli, of simulating irrationality for political survival, distinct from the nuclear-age bargaining application.

whyItMatters: It is a textbook case in the theory of compellence, forcing an opponent to act, as against mere deterrence, and it probes the central Cold War puzzle of how to make suicidal-seeming threats credible, connecting to brinkmanship, commitment, and leaving something to chance. It has regained attention around leaders who project unpredictability as deliberate strategy, and a growing scholarly and journalistic literature debates whether calculated unpredictability helps or harms, making it a live question in the study of coercion.

working.text: recognise that appearing irrational can make believable a threat a rational actor could never credibly issue.
understand that the strategy fails the moment the adversary decides the madness is a bluff.
note that a reputation for irrationality can also undermine your assurances and frighten allies, not only enemies.

limits: The effectiveness of the strategy is genuinely contested, and the evidence that it works is weak and mixed; systematic studies find leaders who tried it generally failed to win the disputes. Appearing irrational can undermine the credibility a leader needs for assurances, since an adversary will not concede if it doubts you will honour a deal, and it can invite pre-emption rather than accommodation and frighten allies who rely on predictability. It also conflicts with standard deterrence theory, which rests on rational, cost-sensitive actors, and recent scholarship identifies distinct failure modes and real domestic political costs to the leader.
misreadings: Nixon did not invent it: the name is Nixon and Haldeman's, but the idea is ancient, from Machiavelli's Brutus, and its Cold War theory belongs to Schelling and Kahn. Schelling did not coin the madman theory; he supplied the bargaining scaffolding of commitment and brinkmanship but did not name or endorse Nixon's application. The 1969 attempts to operationalise it are widely judged to have failed to coerce Hanoi or Moscow. Madman does not mean genuinely mentally ill but a cultivated appearance of irrationality. And the founding quote rests on Haldeman's memoir, which Nixon later disputed.
origin: The name comes from US President Richard Nixon by way of his chief of staff H. R. Haldeman's 1978 memoir 'The Ends of Power'; the underlying logic descends from Thomas Schelling and Herman Kahn, and from Machiavelli's praise of feigned madness.

sources.text: Madman theory, Wikipedia. — the strategy, the Nixon-Haldeman origin, and the disputed effectiveness.
'Madman or Mad Genius? The International Benefits and Domestic Costs of the Madman Strategy' (McManus), Belfer Center. — the scholarly analysis of its failure modes and costs.
